Reviewer #3 Overall Comment: In this manuscript, the authors propose a framework for the joint estimation of SOC and SOH for battery cells undergoing continuous driving cycling under constant and changing temperatures. The pipeline consists of ECM-based adaptive Kalman filtering for SOC estimation, which is enhanced by a first residual learner, giving a first SOH estimation that is improved upon by a second residual learner. Author response: The authors appreciate the reviewer for the careful review and the detailed comments. The comments on the experiment data, methodology, and verifications help us improve the revised manuscript. We have revised the expressions of the proposed two residual learning pipelines as one correction model and one compensation model to interpret the function of each clearly. The two residual learning pipelines work in parallel instead of in series, while the functions are different. The closed-loop monitoring enables continuous monitoring of battery states throughout the entire life span, which is the most important demand of battery management. We have added two more datasets for the evaluation of the proposed models, especially for the unseen real-world loading profiles suggested by the reviewer. We have provided detailed responses to the comments and concerns from the reviewer below, and the revised text is in red in the revised manuscript and supplementary information.

Author response: Thank you for the great suggestion on the background and motivation analysis. As requested, we have added more background descriptions on machine learning based battery monitoring, especially for the most relevant works on residual learning. Although the residual learning has shown great improvement for the battery modeling (Ref. 19) and temperature estimation (Ref. 21), the verifications are conducted on several specific tests instead of for the applications in the whole life monitoring, which is the actual requirement of battery management systems. In addition, the previous works only focus on one kind of modeling pipeline for one specific task, while we generalize the residual learning pipelines with one correction model and one compensation model for clearer model function interpretations (as discussed in the responses to comment 14 below). The incorporation of feature importance analysis helps to understand the mechanistic features that enhance state monitoring, which has not been studied in previous hybrid modeling. In addition, the closed-loop design of the SOC and SOH monitoring enables continuous state monitoring for the whole life span without strict test and complex model calibrations. Finally, we demonstrate the importance of accurate state monitoring and the mechanistic feature extraction to help figure out the potential of thermal issues and battery swelling. In the revised manuscript, we have made the following revisions regarding the residual learning, feature extraction, and model verifications to highlight the gaps and motivations of our models. We also revised the main contribution summary correspondingly. The revised text is in red below.
Introduction Section: Widely adopted methods for battery state monitoring include model-based and data-driven approaches, each offering distinct advantages but also having certain limitations. Model-based methods are known for their robustness, particularly when incorporating high-fidelity models, though they tend to be more complex. In contrast, data-driven methods, which map the relationships between the features and battery states via machine learning (ML) models, offer greater flexibility but often suffer from limited generalization capabilities.11 Consequently, hybrid monitoring structures that combine model-based approaches with machine learning (ML) have gained popularity, aiming to enhance both accuracy and robustness.12–15 One straightforward method involves fusing the outputs of different sub-models to mitigate uncertainties associated with any single model.11,16 Another approach employs filtering techniques following initial estimates from data-driven methods to refine posterior estimates and improve accuracy.17 However, the implementation in SOC estimation adopted the real reference, i.e., coulomb counting, as the observation, which makes it hard to obtain accurate calculations in real applications. On the other hand, ML excels at modeling uncertain relationships, and the estimated errors from model-based methods vary and are hard to describe.18,19 Therefore, the sequential framework of the model-based method followed by ML was proposed.20,21 The main idea is that ML models the uncertainties and the errors of the mechanistic model-based methods, which have been employed for both hybrid battery modeling and temperature estimation. However, the specific model pipeline is designed for a specific purpose and only verified under several specific tests instead of continuous monitoring of battery states for the whole life span. Additionally, physics-informed neural network models have shown the potential to enhance physical interpretability and reduce data requirements in battery modeling.22,23 However, the sensitivity of these models to the tolerance of physical laws can greatly impact their predictive accuracy. Conversely, when reliable prior knowledge is incorporated, data-driven models demonstrate more stable improvements in performance.
Feature extraction is one key factor that hugely influences the accuracy of the ML models.24–28 Methods for statistical calculation can extract highly effective features.24,25 However, these features are often sensitive to varying operating conditions, such as different current rates and temperatures, which can reduce model performance across diverse scenarios. While domain adaptation techniques can reduce the discrepancies between the feature distributions, thus enhancing the generalization of monitoring models under different conditions, they also increase model complexity and computational demands, hindering the application for real-time state estimations.29,30 Therefore, improving the suitability and coherence of features across different conditions is crucial for enhancing model accuracy and generalizability. Additionally, statistical features typically lack physical interpretability, complicating the explanation of ML models. Thus, incorporating features with physical meaning can significantly contribute to more interpretable monitoring systems.31,32 Recent research has increasingly focused on the interpretability of ML models, which provides deeper insights into their internal workings and facilitates better optimization.33–36
Most of the existing work on SOC estimation has been limited to specific operational scenarios, often neglecting performance under real-world conditions where the model must function continuously across a battery's entire lifespan. Health predictions are similarly conducted under idealized conditions, assuming consistent availability of data from uniform charging and discharging cycles—an assumption that is difficult to meet in practical applications. Studies on health monitoring frequently consider ideal scenarios with stable working conditions, while in practice, the varying conditions pose significant challenges to maintaining the effectiveness of monitoring models. The continuous verifications of the SOC and SOH joint estimation model are expected to be conducted entire the whole life span, which is the practical demand of battery management system, instead of under several specific tests. Moreover, battery safety conditions are crucial for monitoring, which is key to avoiding hazards like thermal runaway. The potential of continuous state monitoring during dynamic aging to guide safety warnings worthy deeper studies.
We propose mechanistic leading residual learnings for continuous monitoring of battery states, specifically SOC and SOH, under varying dynamic working conditions throughout the entire lifespan. The general pipeline is adaptable for battery modeling and monitoring for different practical requirements. Using three datasets incorporating different battery types aging under different loading and temperature conditions for verifications, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our model working under different degradation patterns to emulate real-world usage scenarios. The proposed mechanistic leading residual models integrate a model-based approach with ML, where prior estimations and mechanistic features derived from the battery model are used as inputs for residual learners, including a correction model and a compensation model, for enhanced state monitoring. This general pipeline works effectively for both SOC and SOH and constructs a closed-loop framework to support the monitoring of the battery states for the entire life span, regardless of the varying loading profiles, temperature conditions, and working ranges (SOC windows) for representations of uncontrollable, randomly varying, and unseen working scenarios. The model is also beneficial for early thermal safety warnings during aging. Through interpretable ML and practical demonstrations, the proposed model enhances accuracy, robustness, and trustworthiness, thereby increasing its potential for real-world applications. The overall framework is illustrated in Fig. 1, where the pathway of the application and the flowchart of the pipeline for residual learning are demonstrated. Additional model details are provided in Fig. S1.

Data generation subsection: We employed three datasets to evaluate the proposed mechanistic leading residual learning models under dynamic loadings for the full life span. Three types of batteries, including pouch, prismatic, and cylindrical cells, which were cycled with urban, highway, and real-world dynamic profiles, are used for verifications under different scenarios.
To emulate the dynamic working and the varying environmental conditions encountered in real-world applications, the first dataset subjected 13 pouch batteries (nominal capacity of 8 Ah) to aging under dynamic discharge across the entire lifespan at different temperatures.30 Urban, highway, and hybrid profiles were employed and are illustrated in Fig. S2, while Fig. S3 presents the variations in voltage curves observed during the aging process. Capacity degradation curves relative to equivalent full cycles are shown in Fig. S4, demonstrating that urban dynamic loading profiles generally result in longer battery life compared to highway-based loading, with varying temperature conditions significantly affecting the degradation patterns. There are in total 27840 samples (represented as the dynamic discharge cycles) generated in dataset 1.
Besides, 3 large-format prismatic cells with a nominal capacity of 50 Ah are used in the second aging test until they die at around 20% SOH with sudden death, i.e., rapid degradation in a few cycles. We employed WLTP (Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicles Test Procedure) to discharge the cells and used both CC and pulse-constant current (PCC) for charging, as shown in Fig. S5. The pulse was set with an average rate the same as the CC (2 C), while with twice the amplitude. The frequency and duty cycle are 1 Hz and 50%, respectively. The capacity, current, voltage, and temperature curves during aging are shown in Fig. S6. The open circuit voltage (OCV) test was conducted using C/20 constant charging and discharging. The sampling frequency is 10 Hz, and the current and voltage variations for the pulses are tracked precisely. This dataset benefits wide applications, including state monitoring, life prediction, and thermal safety warning. The detailed information of the tested pouch and prismatic cell is listed in Table S1. The sample size, i.e., dynamic discharge curves until capacity drops below 50% of the fresh capacity, is 8590.
Finally, datasets using 25 cylindrical cells from Ref. 37, which were aged with synthetic highway and urban, as well as real city driving profiles, are employed to verify our model for use under different unseen working conditions. Typical current and voltage curves during aging under different loading profiles are shown in Fig. S7, indicating varying discharge patterns observed among different cycling, which therefore cause diverse working scenarios and aging trajectories. We used the first dynamic test after the diagnostic test as the dynamic cycling data during aging, the C/2 discharge capacity before the dynamic cycle as the referenced capacity, and the C/40 discharge curve of a new cell as the OCV curve. There are 483 dynamic discharge curves generated for the model evaluation.
Mechanistic leading residual learning pipelines for enhanced state monitoring subsection: To promote the real-time application of the pipelines, the mechanistic model adopts an equivalent circuit model in this work. For real-time battery SOC estimation, online parameter identification and adaptive filtering methods are employed (see Note S1 for a detailed procedure), where the SOC prior estimations and mechanistic model parameters (e.g., resistance and polarization features) are obtained. Coupled with SOC estimation and coulomb counting for released capacity calculation, the battery capacity can be derived to calculate the prior estimation of battery SOH. Meanwhile, measured parameters (e.g., voltage, current, and released capacity) and identified mechanistic parameters (e.g., identified resistance, OCV, and polarization resistance/capacitance) during dynamic discharging are used to calculate health features, which are composed of several statistical values including mean value, standard deviation, and min and max values of these sequential parameters from a random discharge phase. Detailed feature calculations are described in Methods and Notes S2–S3.

Note S2: In the proposed mechanistic-learning residual learning, we derived three types of features for the machine learning models, namely the prior estimations, the mechanistic features, and the measured features, respectively. The detailed descriptions are below.
Prior estimation features: The prior estimations from the mechanistic model-based filtering are effective in tracking the real values in different scenarios for different battery types. Therefore, the prior estimations from the filtering method serve as the first type of features for the machine learning model.

The polarization resistance and polarization capacitance describe dynamic polarization processes, where the polarization resistance ( ) accounts for charge transfer impedance and concentration polarization, while the polarization capacitance ( ) reflects ion adsorption/desorption at the electrode-electrolyte interface. The time constant ( ) governs the relaxation dynamics of the battery.

The capacity, current, voltage, and temperature curves during aging are shown in Fig. S6. The open circuit voltage (OCV) test was conducted using C/20 constant charging and discharging. The sampling frequency is 10 Hz, and the current and voltage variations for the pulses are tracked precisely. This dataset benefits wide applications, including state monitoring, life prediction, and thermal safety warning. The detailed information of the tested pouch and prismatic cell is listed in Table S1. The sample size, i.e., dynamic discharge curves until capacity drops below 50% of the fresh capacity, is 8590.
Finally, datasets using 25 cylindrical cells from Ref. 37, which were aged with synthetic highway and urban, as well as real city driving profiles, are employed to verify our model for use under different unseen working conditions. Typical current and voltage curves during aging under different loading profiles are shown in Fig. S7, indicating varying discharge patterns observed among different cycling, which therefore cause diverse working scenarios and aging trajectories. We used the first dynamic test after the diagnostic test as the dynamic cycling data during aging, the C/2 discharge capacity before the dynamic cycle as the referenced capacity, and the C/40 discharge curve of a new cell as the OCV curve. There are 483 dynamic discharge curves generated for the model evaluation.
Methods Section: The experimental setup is aimed at emulating real dynamic aging. To this end, three datasets are included in this work. The first dataset includes three different dynamic loading profiles to age pouch batteries (MGL SPIM08HP 8Ah high power pouch cell) under both constant and varying temperature conditions. Specifically, the representative loading profiles for urban (UDDS), highway (HWFET), and hybrid working conditions are employed for discharging, while the multi-constant current charging is used for charging during the aging test.30 The chemistry is nickel cobalt aluminum Oxide (NCA) and graphite, and the voltage limit is 2.8-4.2 V. The loading currents are shown in Fig. S2. Two different temperature conditions including constant temperature (25℃) and variable temperature (15-25-35℃) are set for the testing environment. More details about the experiment and data processing are depicted in Note S5. In the second dataset, we use three large-format prismatic cells (L148N50B 50 Ah), which are widely employed in EVs, for dynamic aging with WLTP profiles. The chemistry is nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC), and the voltage range is set as 2.75-4.3 V. One cell is charged with constant current, and the other employs pulse currents (1 Hz, 50% duty cycle) for charging. The loading currents are shown in Fig. S5, and the aging test is conducted in a thermal chamber with a controlled 35℃. The sampling frequency is set as 10 Hz, which enables the tracking of variations during pulse loadings. The OCV test is conducted with a low current of C/20. The third dataset is from Stanford University, where the cylindrical cells are aged with both synthetic urban and highway dynamic loadings and more practical real-world loading.37 Periodical diagnostic tests are conducted where the real capacities can be obtained. The first dynamic discharge cycle after the diagnostic test is used for the verification where the real capacity can be obtained for verification from the diagnostic test. Furthermore, the sampling frequency is artificially reduced to 0.1 Hz to generate data for the robustness verification of our models in real-world applications.

Reviewer #3 Comment 4: While transparency regarding experimental difficulties is appreciated, some of the challenges experienced by the authors with voltage, current and temperature measurements (Note S4) are not such common occurrences in battery testing and may make the reader question the reliability of the presented experimental dataset.
Author response: It is commonly seen in real-world applications that the data quality is lower than the laboratory measurements, as discussed in many related papers using field datasets. Therefore, in real-world applications, people always need to consider the data preprocessing, where the abnormal data, such as outliers and missing data, are processed. In this work, there are some deficiencies (mainly the missing data) measurements of current, which are processed manually. The processing is conducted at the constant current stages while the data from dynamic loadings is kept. The constant current data filling is easy and reasonable. The proposed models are used in the random dynamic discharging with different loading profiles. Therefore, we believe this data processing is reasonable and necessary regarding real applications and does not influence the evaluations in this paper. There are also some misalignments with the temperature measurements, but we do not use temperature data for the model. This is because not all the cells have a temperature sensor in real-world applications, and we keep the same input for the model in different datasets to evaluate the generalization capability of our models. In addition, we also added the verifications of the proposed method in another two datasets (one experiment dataset and another public dataset from Stanford University (DOI: 10.1038/s41560-024-01675-8)), where the measurements are of good quality. The results proved the effectiveness of our models. In conclusion, we believe that data preprocessing is necessary and common in real-world applications and does not influence the effectiveness evaluation of the proposed models.
Reviewer #3 Comment 5: The authors claim that the employed ML models are grounded on interpretable physical principles, but this is highly debatable. The only ‘physical’ element is the use of the 1-RC ECM as a battery model, which is not properly justified. Many authors have pointed out the shortcomings of RC models and their limited physical insight with respect to internal battery processes. Furthermore, if an ECM is employed in dynamic operation, a consideration of hysteresis voltage modeling should be made.
Author response: The authors thank the reviewer for the question regarding the mechanistic model used in this work. The main function of the mechanistic model in this work is to provide prior estimations of battery SOC and SOH based on conventional filtering methods and extract some mechanistic features, like resistance, polarization resistance, and polarization capacitance. Therefore, we are not aiming at improving the model accuracy while improving the model-based estimations based on the proposed residual learning models and considering the real-time solving in the battery management system. To this end, we adopted the ECM, which can be rapidly calculated during real applications. As the results verified through three different datasets consisting of different battery types, the ECM-based models provide stable estimations, though the accuracy is not high. These estimation errors are compensated by the proposed residual learning models, which largely improve the accuracy for both SOC and SOH under varying verification scenarios. Although the electrochemical meaning of ECM is lower than physical models like P2D and single particle models, it still reflects the ohmic resistance and polarization behaviors of the batteries. Moreover, the real-time identification of the mechanistic features is significant for machine learning, as reflected by the SHAP analysis (Figs. 3 5 and Figs. S21 23), to enable the enhancement of the state estimations. By also comparing with the results that exclude
–
the mechanistic features, as shown in Figs. S11, S18, and S24, the results reveal that mechanistic features are necessary for the machine learning models for the accuracy enhancement. In the revised manuscript, we have revised our title and related content to reflect the main reasons for using the proposed pipeline. The revised text is in red below.
Title: Mechanistic Leading Residual Learning for Battery State Monitoring Entire Full Life
Mechanistic leading residual learning pipelines for enhanced state monitoring subsection: To promote the real-time application of the pipelines, the mechanistic model adopts an equivalent circuit model in this work. For real-time battery SOC estimation, online parameter identification and adaptive filtering methods are employed (see Note S1 for a detailed procedure), where the SOC prior estimations and mechanistic model parameters (e.g., resistance and polarization features) are obtained. Coupled with SOC estimation and coulomb counting for released capacity calculation, the battery capacity can be derived to calculate the prior estimation of battery SOH. Meanwhile, measured parameters (e.g., voltage, current, and released capacity) and identified mechanistic parameters (e.g., identified resistance, OCV, and polarization resistance/capacitance) during dynamic discharging are used to calculate health features, which are composed of several statistical values including mean value, standard deviation, and min and max values of these sequential parameters from a random discharge phase. Detailed feature calculations are described in Methods and Notes S2–S3.

Reviewer #3 Comment 8: ECM parameters are determined online via a forgetting factor RLS algorithm, and it appears as though they are updated every timestep. This undermines any physical foundation that could be present in the first place.
Author response: The mechanistic features, i.e., model parameters from ECM, are extracted every timestep since we employed these features for the SOC estimation, which is also performed every time step. Then, the statistical features of the sequential information of these features are calculated for use in SOH estimation. As demonstrated in the model interpretation results via SHAP analysis (Fig. 3 5) and the comparative results with the estimation outcomes by excluding these
–

Reviewer #3 Comment 9: How is ‘real SOC’ determined? If it is through coulomb counting, then this defeats the purpose of the estimation algorithms.
Author response: The ‘real SOC’ is determined by Coulomb counting, which is a widely adopted way for battery SOC estimation algorithm verifications. The ‘real SOC’ is only used for the comparisons between the estimations from the proposed models and the ‘real’ values to evaluate the estimation accuracy, while it is not used in any part of the modeling or the estimation pipelines. Although coulomb counting can be inaccurate in real-world applications, it can hold high accuracy through the experimental data, and meet the purpose for the model verifications and evaluations. Therefore, the Coulomb counting-based SOC calculation is reasonable for the verification purpose. In the revised manuscript, we added clarifications for the purpose of using Coulomb counting in this work, which is in red text below.

Reviewer #3 Comment 11: There is a risk of circular dependency, as SOC estimation relies on battery capacity (Eq.1), which is updated as a function of the estimated SOC difference (Eq. 4). How is this prevented and how often is capacity updated?
Author response: The updating of battery capacity is vitally important to enable accurate SOC estimation, especially for continuous monitoring of the entire life span. This is also considered in our work, where a closed-loop state updating framework is constructed. The real-time SOC estimation is used for capacity estimation, and the estimated capacity is updated for the SOC estimation in the following discharge cycle, as demonstrated in Fig. 1. Therefore, the continuous monitoring of SOC and SOH during the whole life span under dynamic operations is achieved in this paper, which is not verified in previously related papers. This is proved in the Closed-loop application entire life span section in the revised manuscript, with several test scenarios from the two datasets. The capacity is updated every cycle for dataset 1 and is periodically updated during each RPT test for dataset 3, since we verified the first dynamic discharge after each RPT in dataset 3. We added more descriptions in the revised manuscript and the results for dataset 3, which are also given below in red text.
Introduction Section: We propose mechanistic leading residual learnings for continuous monitoring of battery states, specifically SOC and SOH, under varying dynamic working conditions throughout the entire lifespan. The general pipeline is adaptable for battery modeling and monitoring for different practical requirements. Using three datasets incorporating different battery types aging under different loading and temperature conditions for verifications, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our model working under different degradation patterns to emulate real-world usage scenarios. The proposed mechanistic leading residual models integrate a model-based approach with ML, where prior estimations and mechanistic features derived from the battery model are used as inputs for residual learners, including a correction model and a compensation model, for enhanced state monitoring. This general pipeline works effectively for both SOC and SOH and constructs a closed-loop framework to support the monitoring of the battery states for the entire life span, regardless of the varying loading profiles, temperature conditions, and working ranges (SOC windows) for representations of uncontrollable, randomly varying, and unseen working scenarios. The model is also beneficial for early thermal safety warnings during aging. Through interpretable ML and practical demonstrations, the proposed model enhances accuracy, robustness, and trustworthiness, thereby increasing its potential for real-world applications. The overall framework is illustrated in Fig. 1, where the pathway of the application and the flowchart of the pipeline for residual learning are demonstrated. Additional model details are provided in Fig. S1.
Closed-loop application entire life span subsection: The mechanistic leading residual learners facilitate collaborative monitoring of different battery states throughout the entire lifespan, with capacity updating during each dynamic discharging cycle.
Then, we show the application for dataset 3 with unseen testing conditions under real-world driving profiles. Note that we also use the dynamic cycle after the diagnostic test for verifications, so the degradation curve is composed of sparse points. By using the training cells in Fig. 5a to train the residual learners, the state monitoring under unseen working conditions (cell 92 aged using real-world driving protocols) entire the life span are enhanced, as shown in Fig. 6f. Unseen validation for exemplary cells working under another real city protocols (cell 95) and synthetic Urban + Highway (cell 80) protocols are also shown in Fig. 6f, demonstrating the stability and robustness of our model under varying unseen working conditions, which prove the good extrapolation capability of the proposed mechanistic leading residual learning pipelines.
Numerical results listed in Table S9 indicate the MAE for all the tests is below 1.8% for both SOC and SOH. With enhanced SOC and SOH estimations through closed-loop operations, battery systems are poised for improved management and operational performance. This closed-loop structure not only supports effective state monitoring but also self-updates to maintain functionality and provide safety warnings, thereby optimizing the overall management of the battery system without the need for costly and time-consuming offline testing.

Reviewer #3 Comment 12: Remaining capacity is not a complete measure of battery health, and other indicators, such as degradation modes and impedance growth should be considered. Also, is the OCV profile assumed to remain unchanged during aging?
Author response: Battery aging mode is significant for comprehensive health diagnosis. Our recent paper proposed an interpretable and onboard battery health diagnosis model enabling aging model diagnosis during dynamic operations (arXiv:2503.07383). While the main focus of this work is on the macroscopic charge and health states monitoring, which are required in onboard battery management systems for control purposes. Therefore, we mainly consider capacity degradation monitoring in this work. Though the capacity-based SOH is monitored, we also find the extracted mechanistic features, like resistance, are also significant for describing battery health status, and for guiding warning of thermal issues and battery swelling. We demonstrated this in the revised manuscript by the prismatic cells, which have suffered rapid capacity degradation with increased temperatures and heavy swelling. We admit that degradation mode is significant to help understand the aging mechanisms, while it is not the main focus of this paper. In the revised manuscript, we added some outlooks for future work that incorporate aging mode estimations. One of the main advantages of the proposed machine learning based residual compensations is that the deficiencies from both the model and inaccurate measurements can be compensated. Though OCV at different aging stages helps improve the model accuracy, it is very hard to determine the real SOH value for OCV determination in real applications, i.e., there is still measurement inaccuracy existing. In addition, the OCV curves are also varied with different temperature conditions. Therefore, it will be challenging to consider the coupling influences of aging and temperature in real-world applications, and huge experiment costs will be required. Therefore, only one fresh OCV is required in this paper, while machine learning is expected for the deficiency compensations. The revised text is in red below.
Mechanistic leading residual learning pipelines for enhanced state monitoring subsection:
Here, we introduce mechanistic leading residual learners, incorporating a correction model and a compensation model to enhance the state monitoring results from prior estimations. As shown in Figs. 1b and S8, the prior estimations and extracted features serve as input for the machine learning to output an enhanced estimation and a residual for the prior estimation compensation. Therefore, the function of the correction model is to enhance the prior estimation by direct state predictions, while the compensation model enhances the estimations by adding the predicted residuals to the prior estimations. The prior estimation from the mechanistic model provides stable guidance, and those feature matrices help capture the expected battery states, condition indicators from the real battery responses, as well as the mechanistic features describing the internal conditions. Machine learning is built to compensate for the model uncertainties and other influences like changed OCV under varying conditions; therefore, the OCV and other model parameters do not require careful calibration under temperature and aging. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through two key states: real-time SOC and the more slowly varying SOH. Note that the compared prior estimations represent the conventional model-based filtering methods. The coulomb counting-based calculation is employed to obtain the referenced real SOC and SOH for the evaluations of the conventional model-based filtering method and the proposed residual learning models, while it is not used in any part of the modeling pipelines. Additionally, our model can be easily extended to monitor other relevant states as required, for example, the sensor-less temperature estimations based on the mechanistic features and the lamped-mass thermal model-based prior estimations.21
Varying verifications subsection: We further employed our model for the state monitoring of different battery types with different aging patterns caused by different aging conditions. The dynamic aging of large-format prismatic cells is verified. As shown in Fig. 4a, three large-format prismatic cells are aged with CC/PCC charging and WLTP dynamic discharging, which experience accelerated aging after SOH drops below the knee points. The average current of the pulses remains the same as the constant current, as shown in Fig. 4b. While different battery impedances cause the voltage to vary differently, and according to the heat generation, the cells have higher temperatures using pulse current compared to the constant current. Around 10℃ difference for the maximum temperature and 3.5℃ difference for the average temperature during cycling are seen for the two different charging protocols. These large thermal condition differences during cycling become the main cause of the different lifetimes for the cells under constant or pulse currents. Previous related works have revealed that pulse currents have an influence on battery lifetime. The battery aging is coupled and influenced by current profiles, temperature, current rates, etc., thus, we advocate coupling mechanisms and battery types during evaluations for the lifetime extension strategy designs.
We continuously age the batteries until they die, where accelerated aging is seen. As shown in Fig. S19, the battery is heavily swelled after aging, and the thermal safety issue (largely and rapidly increased temperature) occurred as demonstrated in Fig. 5a. Interestingly, the battery capacity degradation accelerated earlier (around 100 cycles) than the thermal safety issue happened, and the identified mechanistic resistances also show earlier detection. Therefore, accurate estimations of the battery capacity and mechanistic states are also crucial to guide safety management, which helps with early warning of battery safety conditions before thermal issues during operations.
The monitoring results for the cells, until SOH (current capacity divided by initial capacity) drops below 50%, are shown in Figs. 4c d, where the total discharging curves are randomly divided into training and testing datasets with a 50% portion of each. The mechanistic leading correction model
–
and compensation model show improved SOC and SOH monitoring for the full life span with MAE of less than 0.50% and 0.68%, respectively, as listed in Table S4. SHAP interpretation also indicates the most important impact of the prior estimation and reflects the importance of the mechanistic features. Due to the high linear relationships between the corrected and prior estimations, while the higher nonlinear relationships of the residuals between the prior and real estimations, the mechanistic features have higher impacts on the compensation model compared to the correction model. Both models show improved monitoring and reveal the performance of the proposed mechanistic leading residual learning models. More importantly, the potential of early thermal safety warning can be achieved during operation and aging.

Introduction Section: Feature extraction is one key factor that hugely influences the accuracy of the ML models.24–28 Methods for statistical calculation can extract highly effective features.24,25 However, these features are often sensitive to varying operating conditions, such as different current rates and temperatures, which can reduce model performance across diverse scenarios. While domain adaptation techniques can reduce the discrepancies between the feature distributions, thus enhancing the generalization of monitoring models under different conditions, they also increase model complexity and computational demands, hindering the application for real-time state estimations.29,30 Therefore, improving the suitability and coherence of features across different conditions is crucial for enhancing model accuracy and generalizability. Additionally, statistical features typically lack physical interpretability, complicating the explanation of ML models. Thus, incorporating features with physical meaning can significantly contribute to more interpretable monitoring systems.31,32 Recent research has increasingly focused on the interpretability of ML models, which provides deeper insights into their internal workings and facilitates better optimization.33–36
Varying verifications subsection: Overall, we employed our mechanistic leading residual learning with two pipelines for enhanced state monitoring during the whole life span with feature interpretations and validations using different battery types and verification cases, which indicates high generalizations of our models. Nevertheless, the verifications are still conducted separately for the three datasets, though varying conditions are considered. It is still hard for cross-battery material applications since the large discrepancies in the mechanistic features of different batteries. Therefore, the future work needs to further investigate the improved approach enabling applications across different battery types.
Reviewer #3 Comment 19: How is the risk of data leakage treated? Author response: Thank you for the suggestion of a good reference for the discussion of verification in real-world operations. In the revised manuscript, we have incorporated the dataset from the suggested reference for further verification of the model performance under unseen real-world loadings. We also adopted the capacity from the RPT test as the referenced ‘real capacity’ (as asked by the reviewer in comment 10). And the application for the full life monitoring of real-world city loadings is also demonstrated. Specifically, the data from the urban/highway is used for the model training, and the different cells in the same test conditions are employed as validation 1. In addition, the dataset from the cycling with urban + highway is used as validation 2. Furthermore, the cells with real-world city loadings are also verified as validation 3. We even verified the model's performance with reduced sampling frequency (0.1 Hz) to emulate the real-world EV applications. Therefore, we validated several unseen scenarios under real-world applications. The revised text is in red below.
Data generation subsection: Finally, datasets using 25 cylindrical cells from Ref. 37, which were aged with synthetic highway and urban, as well as real city driving profiles, are employed to verify our model for use under different unseen working conditions. Typical current and voltage curves during aging under different loading profiles are shown in Fig. S7, indicating varying discharge patterns observed among different cycling, which therefore cause diverse working scenarios and aging trajectories. We used the first dynamic test after the diagnostic test as the dynamic cycling data during aging, the C/2 discharge capacity before the dynamic cycle as the referenced capacity, and the C/40 discharge curve of a new cell as the OCV curve. There are 483 dynamic discharge curves generated for the model evaluation.
Varying verifications subsection: Finally, cylindrical batteries from Ref. 37 are employed for the verification of the proposed models by considering unseen working conditions. Three different validation cases are generated using cells with different synthetic profiles or real driving profiles aging. Specifically, as shown in Fig. 5a, cells with independent highway or urban loading profiles are divided into a training dataset and the validation 1 dataset. The loading profile of combining highway and urban loadings is included in the validation 2 dataset, and the cells with two city driving profiles are used in the validation 3 dataset. Therefore, we evaluated our mechanistic leading residual learning models with different real applications, considering unseen validation scenarios. Typical loadings and the related prior estimations are demonstrated in Fig. S20. The state monitoring and corresponding interpretation results are shown in Figs. 5bc, respectively. More detailed results for the three validation cases are shown in Figs. S21–S23 and Tables S5–S6. MAE for the SOC estimation keeps below 1.5% for all three validation cases and keeps below 1.8% for SOH estimations for both the correction model and the compensation model. All the cases indicate enhanced state monitoring performance compared to conventional model-based methods, even under unseen loadings for the whole life span. Similar interpretations can be summarized from the SHAP results, i.e., the prior estimations play significant roles for both the correction model and compensation model, while the mechanistic features provide critical information and have higher impacts on the compensation model compared to the correction model. Though the prior estimations are the most significant information, mechanistic parameters are essential for the model, as shown in Fig. S24, where the errors may increase instead by only using prior estimation for the model input.
In real-world applications, the sampling frequency is usually reduced, e.g., 0.1 Hz, so that the estimation accuracy is further deteriorated. The prior estimations with enlarged errors can also be enhanced by our mechanistic leading residual learners. We down-sampled the original data with 0.1 Hz and re-tested the three validation cases to evaluate the robustness of our models in potential real application conditions. The down-sampled currents and original currents (1 Hz) for different loading profiles are shown in Fig. S25, where the currents with 0.1 Hz lost fidelity. Therefore, the prior estimations became worse compared to the results with 1 Hz sampled currents (Fig. 5b), as shown in Fig. S26. Based on the proposed correction model and compensation model, the accuracies are enhanced with MAE less than 1.92% and 3.58% for SOC and SOH monitoring (which are more than 3.4% and 5.5% of filtering based-prior estimations for all the three cases), respectively, demonstrating the effectiveness in low sampling frequency applications. Through model interpretation, we noticed that, though the prior estimations are still the most important information, the accuracy is worse in these cases, which makes the mechanistic features become more important for the model to enhance state monitoring.

The combinations of filtering and machine learning are discussed while citing more related publications, and a more specific motivation is added for better positioning of our work. The revised text is in red below.
Introduction Section: Model-based methods are usually constructed with filtering methods such as the Kalman filter for internal state estimation. In contrast, data-driven methods, which map the relationships between the features and battery states via machine learning (ML) models, offer greater flexibility but often suffer from limited generalization capabilities.11 Consequently, hybrid monitoring structures that combine model-based filtering approaches with ML have gained popularity, aiming to enhance both accuracy and robustness.12–15 One straightforward method involves fusing the outputs of different sub-models, e.g., filtering-based estimation and machine learning estimation, to mitigate uncertainties associated with any single model.11,16,17 Due to the large variances of the estimation from data-driven approaches, especially for SOC estimation, one popular approach employs filtering techniques afterwards to enhance the estimation from ML models.18–21 However, the implementation in SOC estimation usually adopts the real reference, i.e., coulomb counting, as the observation, which makes it hard to obtain accurate calculations in real applications. On the other hand, ML excels at modeling uncertain relationships, and the estimated errors from model-based methods vary and are hard to describe.22,23 Therefore, the sequential framework of the model-based method followed by ML was proposed, where ML is employed after the filtering method to improve the initial estimation from the model-based methods.24–26 The main idea is that ML models the uncertainties and the errors of the mechanistic model-based methods, which have been employed for both hybrid battery modeling and temperature estimation. Nevertheless, the specific pipeline is designed for a specific purpose and has only been verified under several specific tests, limiting its practical large-scale application. Systematic design for general hybrid pipelines integrating model-based filtering and ML methods with applications using dynamic cycling for the entire life span is a practical yet unsolved challenge.

This means the proposed model does not need the periodic calibration cycles or the full discharges for the SOH estimations, which aligns with the requirement for real-world applications. As for the errors for urban+highway profile in Fig. 6f, since we evaluate our models under unseen conditions with machine learning-based approaches, it is common that estimation errors vary. Instead of selecting estimations for specific cells with high accuracy, we give the estimations for randomly selected cells to demonstrate the generalization of the proposed model. We also give the estimations for the other three cells under the same urban+highway loading profiles below, and some cells show better accuracy, and some may have larger errors. Therefore, the errors are mainly caused by machine learning models in some scenarios, which are common for all kinds of machine learning-based approaches. The more important thing is the effectiveness of the proposed models under unseen loading profiles for their whole life with partial and random dynamic discharges.

Though the verification of LFP batteries is missing, we have listed the challenge of the state monitoring of LFP batteries in the discussion and added more specifications regarding hysteresis and flatness. A subsequent validation on unseen constant current and periodic profiles from the same dataset with different pulse frequencies and charge/discharge ratios would substantially enhance the credibility of the proposed methodology, due to their observed impact on aging trajectories.
Author response: Thank you for the suggestion to enhance the verification with more cycling profiles. We mainly focus on enhanced state monitoring under dynamic cycling, which is a significant concern in real-world electric vehicle applications. The added verifications using the Stanford dataset also contain unseen conditions, e.g., the training using Highway and Urban synthetic profiles for the state estimation of cells aged with real-world city profiles. Constant current and periodic profiles, though they have a vital impact on aging trajectories, are not widely seen in real-world electric vehicle applications. Since periodic profiles are also seen in other applications such as grid energy storage, we added the applications to the verifications on the cells with periodic profiles to further evaluate the extrapolation capability of the proposed model for unseen conditions. Specifically, the model trained from the same training cells in Fig. 5a is applied to verify cells aged with “Charge-Discharge Ratio”, “High Current Amplitude”, and “Frequency” periodic profiles under both C/10 and C/5 from the Stanford dataset. We added a supplementary figure and the description text in red below.
Varying verifications subsection: We have verified the models using real-world driving cycles for potential real-world EV applications. To further evaluate the model extrapolation to other application scenarios such as grid storage, we applied the same model trained based on the training cells in Fig. 5a for the verification of cells aged with three different kinds of periodic profiles. The results for the SOC and SOH monitoring are shown in Fig. S28, indicating the effectiveness of the proposed model for accuracy enhancement even under quite different unseen loading profiles and aging trajectories.
Fig. S28. Extrapolation verification to the periodic profiles with “Charge-Discharge Ratio”, “High Current Amplitude”, and “Frequency” under C/5 and C/10. a. SOH error distributions of the filtering-based method and the two residual learning models. d. RMSE and MAE of the SOH estimation results.

Reviewer #3 Major Comment 2: The authors argue that 'only one fresh OCV is required in this paper, while machine learning is expected for the deficiency compensations'. This is a strong claim, especially when more advanced degradation stages are considered, which can substantially alter the shape of the OCV. The implications of this assumption on estimation accuracy should be fully discussed in order to properly justify this claim.
Author response: We thank the reviewer for the careful review and questions. In this work, we only used the fresh OCV in estimations of both SOC and SOH over the whole lifespan, i.e., the whole cycling data from the datasets, even with SOH drops below 50% for dataset 2. We agree that the OCV curve shapes will change during aging, especially for the silicon-graphite anode cells in dataset 3. However, even for dataset 3, we also only used one OCV curve from the first RPT test for the estimations until the end of cycling, and the results indicate the good performance of the proposed models. In addition, the OCV also changed under different temperatures and other conditions in real applications, and we also proved our model under variable temperature conditions in dataset 1. Therefore, the proposed residual learning models are expected to learn the residuals caused by model-based methods, which include the one caused by the OCV variations during aging. This has been verified with the three datasets of different batteries aged under different conditions. It is also more promising for real-world applications with fewer degrees of freedom in variables and lower data availability. In addition, the authors also noticed the deficiencies of the OCV models during aging and are currently investigating similar residual compensations for improved OCV fitting during aging, which will be published in our upcoming paper. In the revised manuscript, we revised the following red text for clarification.
Mechanistic leading residual learning pipelines for enhanced state monitoring subsection:
The ML model is built to compensate for the error caused by model uncertainties and other influences such as OCV variations under varying aging and temperature conditions.
Varying verifications subsection: Only one fresh OCV curve is used for the estimations instead of updating during aging, which would require more tests and need further calibrations in real-world applications, and the results indicate the residual models are effective to learn the change during aging for accuracy enhancement.
Reviewer #3 Major Comment 3: Authors compare the estimation accuracy of the proposed methodology to that of the conventional model-based filtering approach. However, a comparison in computational efficiency is lacking, despite it being the other main factor for real-time monitoring in a practical BMS application. The computational overhead due to the addition of the ML models should be quantified and the tradeoff between accuracy and computational complexity should be discussed.
Author response: Thanks for the suggestion on computation cost evaluation regarding potential real applications. In our work, we avoid complex deep learning methods, instead employing a simpler machine learning method (Random Forest regression). This kind of machine learning method was expected to have fast execution after training with a low-dimensional feature vector for each estimation step. To evaluate this exectation, we include the computational costs in an additional Supplementary figure (S31) for the three application studies in Fig. 6F. The time for each point is the total estimation time of the full discharge curve running on a laptop (13th Gen Intel(R) CoreTM i9-13950HX, 2.20 GHz, 128 GB). As Figure S31 shows, the additional computation cost for machine learning is acceptable, with a relatively constant time because, when the model is trained, the input feature matrix keeps the same dimension for usage. The time difference between the three figures is mainly caused by different C-rates and battery aging. It shows that the additional computation time for more than 20,000 data points (loading profiles shown in Fig. S7) is less than 1 second, indicating the potential for real applications. We have inserted the below red text into the revised manuscript and the supplementary figure.
Closed-loop application entire life span subsection: Furthermore, we evaluate the computational cost for consideration of practical application. The execution time for the full discharge at each SOH point in Fig. 6f is shown in Fig. S31. Due to the low dimension of features and with a simple machine learning model, only a slight additional time (less than 1 second for the full discharge) is required for the residual learning models for accuracy enhancement.
Fig. S31. Execution time for each discharge curve during the aging for the three cells aged under City 1, City 2, and Highway+Urban profiles is in a-c, respectively.

Reviewer #3 Minor Comment 1: Although the authors provide more context in the revised introduction, some background and shortcomings of the combination of Kalman Filters and Machine Learning would greatly aid in better positioning this work with respect to state of the art.
Author response: As requested, more background and shortcomings of the combination of Kalman filters and machine learning have been inserted into the revised manuscript. The combinations of filtering and machine learning are discussed while citing more related publications, and a more specific motivation is added for better positioning of our work. The revised text is in red below.
Introduction Section: Model-based methods are usually constructed with filtering methods such as the Kalman filter for internal state estimation. In contrast, data-driven methods, which map the relationships between the features and battery states via machine learning (ML) models, offer greater flexibility but often suffer from limited generalization capabilities.11 Consequently, hybrid monitoring structures that combine model-based filtering approaches with ML have gained popularity, aiming to enhance both accuracy and robustness.12–15 One straightforward method involves fusing the outputs of different sub-models, e.g., filtering-based estimation and machine learning estimation, to mitigate uncertainties associated with any single model.11,16,17 Due to the large variances of the estimation from data-driven approaches, especially for SOC estimation, one popular approach employs filtering techniques afterwards to enhance the estimation from ML models.18–21 However, the implementation in SOC estimation usually adopts the real reference, i.e., coulomb counting, as the observation, which makes it hard to obtain accurate calculations in real applications. On the other hand, ML excels at modeling uncertain relationships, and the estimated errors from model-based methods vary and are hard to describe.22,23 Therefore, the sequential framework of the model-based method followed by ML was proposed, where ML is employed after the filtering method to improve the initial estimation from the model-based methods.24–26 The main idea is that ML models the uncertainties and the errors of the mechanistic model-based methods, which have been employed for both hybrid battery modeling and temperature estimation. Nevertheless, the specific pipeline is designed for a specific purpose and has only been verified under several specific tests, limiting its practical large-scale application. Systematic design for general hybrid pipelines integrating model-based filtering and ML methods with applications using dynamic cycling for the entire life span is a practical yet unsolved challenge.
Reviewer #3 Minor Comment 2: In Fig. 6f (urban+highway), the SOH estimation results are less accurate from 0 to 1000 EFCs. Could this be due to the fact that RPTs were conducted every 100 cycles? If so, authors should discuss the applicability of the methodology in real-world operation during which periodic calibration cycles or full discharges are not available or more sparsely distributed in time.
Author response: Thanks for the careful review and questions. The proposed method adopted random and partial discharge curves for the SOH estimation, and the model is applicable to dynamic profiles. All these three aspects are the main concerns regarding real-world EV operations. In addition, as discussed above, only fresh OCV is required for modeling. This means the proposed model does not need the periodic calibration cycles or the full discharges for the SOH estimations, which aligns with the requirement for real-world applications. As for the errors for urban+highway profile in Fig. 6f, since we evaluate our models under unseen conditions with machine learning-based approaches, it is common that estimation errors vary. Instead of selecting estimations for specific cells with high accuracy, we give the estimations for randomly selected cells to demonstrate the generalization of the proposed model. We also give the estimations for the other three cells under the same urban+highway loading profiles below, and some cells show better accuracy, and some may have larger errors. Therefore, the errors are mainly caused by machine learning models in some scenarios, which are common for all kinds of machine learning-based approaches. The more important thing is the effectiveness of the proposed models under unseen loading profiles for their whole life with partial and random dynamic discharges.

Author response: In our manuscript, we have shown the identified resistance variations during aging to show the earlier thermal warning capabilities in Fig. 4a. In the revised manuscript, we also insert a supplementary figure (S10) to demonstrate the variations of the ECM parameters over the dynamic discharge cycle during the degradations under different loading profiles. Author response: Thanks for the suggestion. We have inserted a statement on the estimated capacity in this work, which is the available capacity under specific working conditions, to avoid confusion with the standard capacity that is generally defined with the RPT test. The revised text is in red below.

The capacity here represents the releasable discharge capacity under the corresponding discharging condition with specific loading profile, temperature, and aging conditions.
Reviewer #3 Minor Comment 5: As suggested by Reviewer 2, SOC estimation on NMC or NCA chemistries poses fewer challenges due to a greater slope of the OCV and smaller hysteresis voltage. The applicability of this methodology and potential challenges should be briefly discussed specifically for LFP, taking into account its particular features such as a flat OCV and considerable voltage hysteresis.
Author response: The authors thank the reviewer for the question. As we responded to Reviewer 2’s comment in the first-round revision, we admit the challenge of state estimation of LFP batteries, especially due to their hysteresis and OCV flatness. In this work, we aimed at the systematic design of mechanistic-leading residual learning models with applications to state monitoring the entire life span. We verified the effectiveness of the proposed models using different batteries with varying aging conditions that emulate real-world applications. The extrapolation has also been verified for several unseen conditions. Though the verification of LFP batteries is missing, we have listed the challenge of the state monitoring of LFP batteries in the discussion and added more specifications regarding hysteresis and flatness. In addition, our group is currently studying a similar residual learning pipeline in battery modeling for LFP batteries to handle the challenges of hysteresis and flatness, similar to the model uncertainties discussed in this manuscript, and we have also inserted this statement as future work in the revised manuscript. The revised text is in red below.
Results section: It is still hard for cross-battery material applications due to the large discrepancies in the mechanistic features of different batteries caused by the chemical properties. Therefore, future work needs to further investigate the improved approach enabling applications across different battery types, especially for lithium-ion phosphate batteries, which pose a significant challenge to address the impact of hysteresis and OCV flatness in state estimations. In addition, the proposed mechanistic leading hybrid modeling framework is worthy of investigation for improving the electrochemical model fidelity.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Battery monitoring requires high accuracy and robustness throughout the entire lifespan to ensure safe and optimal operations. Here we introduce mechanistic leading residual learners to enhance the monitoring of battery charge and health states, as well as guide safety warnings, targeting large-scale applications. Leveraging prior knowledge from real-time filtering as primary guidance, complemented by mechanistic and statistical features, our approach significantly improves accuracy and robustness. We propose and validate two general residual learning pipelines, namely the correction model and compensation model, across various scenarios, encompassing different battery types, loading profiles, aging conditions, and environmental conditions, using three aging datasets under dynamic cycling. Our method achieves a relative root mean square error reduction of over 50% from the results observed in prior estimations. The extrapolation capability under unseen conditions, along with interpretability, enhances both accuracy and trustworthiness. The models remain effective even with reduced training data and sampling frequency, maintaining the potential for practical electric vehicle applications. Application demonstrations confirm the efficacy in providing continuous monitoring across lifespan without the need for offline testing and model calibration during operation.

---

## Introduction

Lithium-ion batteries are extensively utilized to support sustainable development, yet they present significant challenges in accurate state monitoring due to their diverse chemistry and types, usage conditions, and the complex aging processes encountered in electrified transportation1–4. To ensure safe operations and guide optimal management, state of charge (SOC) and state of health (SOH) are two of the most concerned indices to indicate the battery potential in real-time and in a long-time horizon5–7. Developing a closed-loop framework for battery monitoring is crucial for enhancing battery management and avoiding safety hazards, particularly as batteries degrade8–10. Traditionally, specific tests are conducted to verify the estimations of SOC and SOH independently or under several sparse conditions. However, real-world applications demand effective battery state monitoring that accounts for continuous aging under dynamic loads and varying temperatures.

Widely adopted methods for battery state monitoring include model-based and data-driven approaches, each offering distinct advantages but also having certain limitations. Model-based methods are known for their robustness, particularly when incorporating high-fidelity battery models, though they tend to be more complex. Model-based methods are usually constructed with filtering methods such as the Kalman filter for internal state estimation. In contrast, data-driven methods, which map the relationships between the features and battery states via machine learning (ML) models, offer greater flexibility but often suffer from limited generalization capabilities11. Consequently, hybrid monitoring structures that combine model-based filtering approaches with ML have gained popularity, aiming to enhance both accuracy and robustness12–15. One straightforward method involves fusing the outputs of different sub-models, e.g., filtering-based estimation and ML estimation, to mitigate uncertainties associated with any single model11,16,17. Due to the large variances of the estimation from data-driven approaches, especially for SOC estimation, one popular approach employs filtering techniques afterward to enhance the estimation from ML models16,18–20. However, the implementation in SOC estimation usually adopts the real reference, i.e., coulomb counting, as the observation, which makes it hard to obtain accurate calculations in real applications. On the other hand, ML excels at modeling uncertain relationships, and the estimated errors from model-based methods vary and are hard to describe21,22. Therefore, the sequential framework of the model-based method followed by ML was proposed, where ML is employed after the filtering method to improve the initial estimation from model-based methods23–25. The main idea is that ML models the uncertainties and the errors of the mechanistic model-based methods, which have been employed for both battery modeling and temperature estimation. Nevertheless, the specific pipeline is designed for a specific purpose and has only been verified under several specific tests, limiting its practical large-scale application. Systematic design for general hybrid pipelines integrating model-based filtering and ML methods with applications using dynamic cycling for the entire lifespan is a practical yet unsolved challenge. Additionally, physics-informed neural network models have shown the potential to enhance physical interpretability and reduce data requirements in battery modeling26,27. However, the sensitivity of these models to the tolerance of physical laws can greatly impact their predictive accuracy. Conversely, when reliable prior knowledge is incorporated, data-driven models demonstrate more stable improvements in predictive performance.

Feature extraction is one key factor that hugely influences the accuracy of ML models28–32. Methods for statistical calculation can extract highly effective features28,29. However, these features are often sensitive to varying operating conditions, such as different current rates and temperatures, which can reduce model performance across diverse scenarios. While domain adaptation techniques can reduce the discrepancies between the feature distributions, thus enhancing the generalization of monitoring models under different conditions, they also increase model complexity and computational demands, hindering the application for real-time state estimation33,34. Therefore, improving the suitability and coherence of features across different conditions is crucial for enhancing model accuracy and generalizability. Additionally, statistical features typically lack physical interpretability, complicating the explanation of ML models. Thus, incorporating features with mechanistic meaning can significantly contribute to more interpretable monitoring systems35,36. Recent research has increasingly focused on the interpretability of ML models, which provides deeper insights into their internal workings and facilitates better optimization37–40.

Most of the existing work on SOC estimation has been limited to specific operational scenarios, often neglecting performance under real-world conditions where the model must function continuously across a battery’s entire lifespan. Health predictions are similarly conducted under idealized conditions, assuming consistent availability of data from uniform charging and discharging cycles, an assumption that is difficult to meet in practical applications. Studies on health monitoring frequently consider ideal scenarios with stable working conditions, while in practice, the varying conditions pose significant challenges to maintaining the effectiveness of monitoring models. The continuous verifications of the SOC and SOH joint estimation model are expected to be conducted during the entire lifespan, which is the practical demand of the battery management system, instead of under several specific tests. Moreover, battery safety conditions are crucial for monitoring, which is key to avoiding hazards like thermal runaway. The potential of continuous state monitoring during dynamic aging to guide safety warnings worthy deeper studies.
